bio.en: Geoffrey Moore is the author of Crossing the Chasm, perhaps the most influential book ever written on technology go-to-market strategy, and a longtime advisor to B2B and tech companies on scaling through the adoption lifecycle.
bio.zh: Geoffrey Moore 是《跨越鸿沟》（Crossing the Chasm）的作者，这本书堪称史上最具影响力的技术产品上市策略著作，他长期为 B2B 与科技公司提供跨越采用生命周期、实现规模化的咨询。

summary.en: Geoffrey uses the 'kindling vs. log' metaphor to explain why, when stuck in the chasm, taking any customer you can find is a mistake—you need to light a fire in one narrow place first. He lays out the bowling-pin strategy for getting past early adopters, the specific go-to-market playbook for each stage of the adoption lifecycle, and the seven deadly sins of crossing the chasm incorrectly. The conversation also covers how to sell to different personas (and why early adopters don't need you to focus on problem and pain) plus some unexpected life advice.
summary.zh: Geoffrey 用“引火物 vs. 原木”的比喻说明：当卡在鸿沟（chasm）中时，来者不拒地抓客户是错的——你需要先在一个狭窄的点上把火点着。他讲解了用“保龄球瓶”策略越过早期采用者、针对不同采用生命周期阶段的特定上市打法，以及跨越鸿沟时最常见的七宗罪。对话还涵盖了如何向不同人物角色销售（以及为何对早期采用者无需执着于“问题”和“痛点”），并附带一些出乎意料的人生建议。

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: The tendency when you're in the chasm is, "I just need more customers. I should take any customer I could find," because we need revenue. It's like taking a match and running it back and forth under a log. It's not going to light the log. So how do you start a fire? Well, you start it by putting a little kindling, little crumpled up paper, and you hold the match in one place until the fire starts. That's why adjacency is so important. If you light the fire, the piece of kindling is here, but the log is in the other room. That doesn't work.
turns.zh: 身处深渊时，人们往往会想：“我只需要更多客户。能拉到一个客户就应该抓住。” 毕竟我们急需营收。但这就像拿火柴在木头下来回摩擦——根本点不着火。那么如何点燃火堆呢？关键在于先放置一些引火柴，比如揉皱的纸片，然后把火柴固定在一个位置，直到火势渐起。这就是邻近性为何至关重要的原因。假如你点燃了火堆，但引火柴在另一个房间，火势就无法延续。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's incredibly cool to have you on. You've been at the top of my wishlist of guests to have on this podcast ever since I launched it, so it's surreal to be chatting with you. It almost feels like maybe this podcast has crossed the chasm now that you're on.
turns.zh: 你能来真是太棒了。自从我推出这个播客以来，你就一直是我最想邀请的嘉宾之一。现在你终于来了，感觉太不可思议了。这几乎让我觉得，也许这个播客现在已经突破了瓶颈。

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: If you'd called me earlier, I probably would've been on it with you. But anyway, we're together now.
turns.zh: 如果你早点联系我，我很可能就会和你一起上节目了。但无论如何，我们现在终于见面了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I thought it'd be fun to start with this question of just what frustrates you most about what people still don't get about the things that you teach, particularly Crossing the Chasm. You wrote that, I think, 33 years ago at this point. You have a lot of follow-up books around the topic. What do you think people still don't really understand or often get wrong?
turns.zh: 我想先从这个问题开始——你对人们仍然不理解你所教授的内容，最感到沮丧的是什么？特别是《跨越鸿沟》这本书。你写这本书已经33年了，对吧？你还写了很多后续的书籍。你认为人们仍然不理解或经常误解什么？

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: All the books I write are about frameworks. They're conceptual models about what patterns should you be looking for as something evolves? Because in disruptive innovation, there's no history. You're always projecting a possible history, and then seeing if you can make it come true. So that implies there's a lot of freedom to exercise the framework however you choose to. People sometimes do that in ways that are just... They actually end up being very misleading about what's possible. I can remember one person early on saying, "Yeah, we're Crossing the Chasm. Our beachhead segments the Fortune 500," and you went, "Well, I don't think maybe you're as clear on this as you could be." (00:05:32): To be fair, that's what the function of any third party advisor is, is to say, "Look, time out. You might be looking at this through an inside-out lens. Maybe you should be looking at it from an outside-in lens." That's probably number one. Gosh, after that, I'm just empathetic with the fact that their world's more important than my world, so I try to work with their world.
turns.zh: 我写的所有书都是关于框架的。它们是概念性模型，告诉你当某件事发展时，应该寻找哪些模式？因为在颠覆性创新中，没有历史可参考。你总是在预测可能的历史轨迹，然后看看能否让它成真。这意味着你可以自由地按照自己的方式应用这些框架。但有时人们的做法会让人误解可能性。我记得早期有人说：“是啊，我们正在跨越鸿沟。我们的滩头阵地是《财富》500强企业。”你当时就说：“嗯，我觉得你可能理解得不太清楚。”（00:05:32）公平地说，这就是任何第三方顾问的职责所在，就是说：“听着，请暂停一下。你可能是在用内向型视角看问题，也许你应该用外向型视角看问题。”这可能是最重要的一点。天哪，之后我就会对他们的世界比我的更重要这一事实心怀同理，所以我会努力适应他们的世界。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's exactly where I actually wanted to go next is this idea of starting very focused with your initial target audience. I think people conceptually know this. They're like, "Yeah, we should be really focused with our initial target market. We should stay very small, and expand this beachhead idea." But I think they still don't quite actually do this because it's like, "Why not go wider?" So could you just talk about why that is so important, and how to actually think about how to do that correctly?
turns.zh: 这正是我接下来想讨论的——从一开始就高度聚焦于你的初始目标受众。我觉得人们在概念上都知道这一点。他们会说：“是啊，我们应该真正专注于我们的初始目标市场。我们应该保持规模小，然后扩展这个滩头阵地。”但我觉得他们还是做不到这一点，因为他们会想：“为什么不扩大范围呢？” 你能谈谈为什么这如此重要，以及如何正确地思考如何做到这一点吗？

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: If you're essentially in a business where the category is emerging, then the most important thing for you to do is to be able to create enough power around your company that you can navigate your future on your own power. Where does power come from in an early adopting technology world? First of all, it'll come from can you get a lighthouse customer? So one of the things we try to do even before you try to cross the chasm is can you get one or more customers who put you on the map? And they go, "Whoa, did you know that the CIA used AWS?" Like, "Holy smoke." Okay, that's great. It doesn't make a company, but it makes a story, and it lets people know, "Oh, here are the guys that did the CIA project," that kind of thing. (00:07:09): The Crossing the Chasm model is, "Can you create a viable repeatable business?" And in order to do that, you need to have an ecosystem of partners work with you in order to consolidate your position. Well, why would an ecosystem work with some startup that nobody's ever heard of? The answer would be if you had consolidated a market segment where you were number one. So one of the things we've learned about company power is that basically it's the company power plus the ecosystem together. So ecosystems form around market leaders, and they do not form around the rest of us. If you're a category leader, if you're like Oracle and Databases, you're 40 years in. You're still the leader, because the ecosystem organized around you. (00:07:51): But when you're little, the only way you can get an ecosystem to organize around you is to go after a segment where you're a big fish in that pond. We talk a lot about fish to pond ratio. You want to be... Your first pond, your target segment should be something that in the next two years, if you hit your really high growth rates, you could be 30, 40, 50% of the market share in that segment. That would cause partners to go, "Whoa, if we're going to serve that segment, we got to work with these guys." So that's the key. The concept there is, "Well, why wouldn't you also do two or three or four segments at the same time?" It's sort of the same reason, "Why wouldn't you run in three or four primaries at the same time if you want the presidential nomination?" Although why you would want that nomination, I have no idea. (00:08:39): But if you did, you realize if you're running in New Hampshire, votes in Vermont do not count. It's the same thing with Crossing the Chasm. You need to get three or four or five or six reputable companies in a segment to all pick you, for then the rest of the segment to go, "Well, it's pretty obvious who the standard is." I'll just close with one last comment. And the reason, the mechanism behind all that logic, is that pragmatic people buy what they see their peers are buying. So if peer one is buying product A, and peer two is B and C and D, there's no market leader, and the category goes sideways. But if A, B and C, if three out of four people are using the iPhone, it's like, "Oh, I guess I'm supposed to get an iPhone," that kind of thing.
turns.zh:
假设你所处的行业正处于新兴阶段，那么最重要的是要为公司创造足够的影响力，让你能凭借自身实力开拓未来。在早期采用新技术的领域，影响力从何而来？首先，你能否获得一个标杆客户？比如，在你试图跨越鸿沟之前，我们会先问：你能否找到一个或多个客户，让他们认可你的价值？他们可能会惊呼：“哇，你知道中情局用AWS吗？！”或者惊呼：“天哪！”这很棒，虽然这本身并不能成就一家公司，但能创造一个故事，让人们知道“哦，原来是他们做的中情局项目！”之类的。（00:07:09）  
“跨越鸿沟”模型的问题在于：“你能否建立可重复的可行业务？”为此，你需要生态系统中的合作伙伴协同巩固你的地位。但为什么生态系统会与一家无人知晓的小型初创公司合作呢？答案是，当你已在某个细分市场占据头把交椅时，生态系统才会围绕你形成。例如，甲骨文在数据库领域深耕40年，至今仍是领导者，因为整个生态系统围绕它而建立。  
（00:07:51）  
但当你规模较小时，唯一能让生态系统围绕你形成的办法，就是在某个细分市场中成为该领域的巨头。我们常说的“鱼与池塘比例”概念至关重要。你的首个池塘、目标细分市场应能让你在未来两年内凭借高增长率占据该细分市场的30%、40%或50%份额。这样合作伙伴才会说：“哇，如果我们要服务这个细分市场，就必须与这些家伙合作。”这才是关键。  
但有人会问：“为什么不同时布局两三个细分市场呢？” 原因与竞选总统提名类似：如果你同时在多个州参选，选民会困惑投票给谁。但如果你只专注于新罕布什尔州，佛蒙特州的选票就不算数。  
在“跨越鸿沟”理论中，要在一个细分市场中获得三到六家知名公司的认可，然后整个细分市场才会认可标准。  
最后总结一点：这一切背后的逻辑机制是，务实的人会追随同行的选择。例如，如果同行选用产品A，而B、C、D也选用A，那么市场就会停滞不前。但如果四分之三的人使用iPhone，人们就会效仿：“哦，看来我也该用iPhone了。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I'm glad you went there, because that's essentially the root of this Crossing the Chasm idea that people after the chasm, the pragmatists, wait for references and social proof, and they're waiting for someone to tell them, "This is worth using," versus visionaries right before the chasm. They're like, "I just want to use the future. I need to be there before anyone else."
turns.zh: 太棒了。很高兴你能深入探讨这个问题，因为这正是“跨越鸿沟”理念的核心——鸿沟过后的人群，即务实派，会等待参考案例和社会认同，等待有人告诉他们“这个值得使用”，而非鸿沟前的愿景派。他们会说：“我只想用未来的产品，我必须比别人先行一步。”

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: You're right. One of the ways we try to capture that in a thought bubble is before the chasm, the customers you work with are people who say, "We believe what you believe." So in other words, they're on the same side. After the chasm, they say, "I'm not sure about that, but we need what you have." So transitioning from, "We believe what you believe," which is how you sell to visionaries to, "We need what you have," which is how you sell to pragmatists. That's the shift.
turns.zh: 你说得对。我们试图在思维泡泡中捕捉这种转变的方式之一，就是在“鸿沟”出现之前，与你合作的客户会说：“我们认同你的理念。”换句话说，他们与你立场一致。而跨越“鸿沟”之后，他们会说：“我对此不太确定，但我们需要你提供的解决方案。” 因此，从“我们认同你的理念”（这是向有远见者推销的方式），到“我们需要你提供的解决方案”（这是向实用主义者推销的方式），这就是转变所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's actually spend some more time there on what it is that each of these segments needs, and how you convince them to use it, because this is really useful. So in these pragmatists group, you're saying the pitch there is you have a pain. I will solve this pain, and it's important pain. I think people always assume that's the pitch. But interestingly, your point is earlier in the two segments and maybe share what those two are, they use your product for a different reason.
turns.zh: 接下来，我们可以花更多时间探讨这两个客户群体各自的需求，以及如何说服他们使用你的产品，因为这确实很有用。对于实用主义者群体，你提到推销话术是：“你存在一个痛点，我能解决这个痛点，而且这个痛点很重要。” 我觉得人们通常会认为这就是标准的推销说辞。但有趣的是，你提到在前两个客户群体中，他们使用你的产品的原因有所不同。

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: In fact, if there's a total in the model of the technology adoption lifecycle that we organize this all around, there's actually four, I call them, inflection points. The first one we call the early market. That's the one we were talking... That's the visionaries and the technology enthusiasts. They are as excited about you as you are. I mean, they want the demo. They want to see the vision. They're exciting. And the key to that market is to have an executive sponsor who has enough clout to essentially fund this thing, because there's no budget for you. So they've got to create the funding, and then drive the organization to go all the way to bright. (00:11:21): They're not that many visionary customers, but there's always one or two. The reason why it's so important to work with a marquee customer then is you... Look, nobody's ever heard of you, and if they've never heard of your customer, I don't care how amazing the win is. Nobody's going to hear about it. So it's really important you did it with Apple, or you did it with Verizon, or you did it with Mercedes, somebody that people have heard. So that's number one, and that's a project model. Even if what you sell is a product, those early mark... Every one of them is kind of a snowflake. It needs a ton of special services. There's no ecosystem of partners to support you, so you throw a bunch of extra labor at it. You do whatever, because you got to make them successful. So you'll do whatever it takes. (00:12:13): Okay, very cool. Got my marquee client, not scalable business, I mean, obviously. So then the second one is the Crossing the Chasm playbook. That's the one that organizes around the problem. The good news is those customers are open to hearing from someone new, because they've already talked to everybody they already know, and the problem is still... It's not that it's unsolved. It's being solved in a crummy way and, by the way, in a deteriorating crummy way. So it's getting actually worse. So there's pressure for them to act. This is where you go from the project model to the solution model, and as a vendor, you over commit to their problem. (00:12:54): From the very beginning, you talk to them. They don't want to talk to you about you. They want to talk to you about them, and you need to ask them probing questions about them. Just like going to a doctor, you don't want the doctor to come and say, "Hey, can I show you a movie of the operation I just did? I want to give you a demo. You mind if I give you a demo?" It's like, "No. What I would like to do is talk to you about this pain I have in my side." And then when the doctor asks you good questions about it, you go, "Ah, this is a good doctor. I'm going to trust this." So that's the whole point about that. Again, that scales a lot more than a project business, but it only scales up to the limit of the target segment. (00:13:31): So we had this bowling alley model of extending. You could go to a second segment, a third segment if it was adjacent. Adjacent means either it's the same customer with a different use case, or it's the same use case in a different customer base, because the one case, you use your customer references. The other case, you use your partners, because the partners who built the one use case will say, "Well, we got another segment that we work with. Let's bring you into that segment too." So that can take a company from, I don't know, tens of millions of dollars to hundreds of millions of dollars in the bowling alley. And in specialized industries like computer-rated design or things like that, you can actually go to a billion dollars or higher. (00:14:13): But with most other categories, at some point, you have this third inflection point, which is it's when people go, "Well, wait a minute, wifi isn't just for financial analysts, or isn't just for... Wifi is for everybody." So instead of saying, "We believe what you believe," which we're not there anymore. And these people aren't even really saying, "We need what you have." What they're saying is, "We want what they have. This is really cool. I want what they have," and that creates what we call the tornado. That's when people... This is when you do want sales coverage, and you do want to go broad, and you do want to have a standard product. Basically, you want to capture as much market share as you can. There's a whole playbook around doing that, which was in a book called Inside the Tornado. (00:15:02): And then the last one, which is actually becoming much more important in this century is called Main Street, but Main Street where products have become commoditized, services become the new place of innovation. We've had taxis for 100 years, but Uber is an incredibly valuable thing. You convert the product to the service, and how do you revolutionize services? That's a situation where now people are saying, "Look, I don't want to own the product. I don't want to own it." Well, kids, "I don't want to own a car. I just want to call Uber. It's convenient." So anyway, those are the four models, and Crossing the Chasm was about that second one.
turns.zh:
事实上，如果我们以技术采用生命周期模型为核心来梳理整个过程，实际上有四个关键节点，我称之为"转折点"。第一个阶段我们称之为"早期市场"。这正是我们之前讨论的阶段——由有远见的人和技术爱好者组成。他们对你的产品充满热情，我是说他们渴望看到演示，领略愿景，激情四射。关键在于，必须有一位有足够影响力的高管赞助者来为项目提供资金支持，因为你的预算根本不足。所以他们必须自己筹集资金，并推动整个组织全力推进项目。（00:11:21）：这类有远见的客户并不多见，但总会有那么一两个。与此同时，与大牌客户合作至关重要，因为没人听说过你，而如果你的客户名气不大，即便成果再惊艳，也无人问津。因此，与苹果、威瑞森或梅赛德斯等知名品牌合作意义非凡。这是第一个阶段，属于项目型模式。即使你卖的是产品，早期市场客户也各不相同，需要投入大量定制化服务，缺乏成熟的合作伙伴生态系统，因此必须投入大量额外人力去支持项目。（00:12:13）：好的，明白了。有了大牌客户，但业务不可扩展，显然如此。接下来是"跨越鸿沟"策略。这阶段以解决问题为核心。好消息是这些客户乐于听取新方案，因为他们已把认识的人都找遍了，而问题依然存在——并非未解决，而是解决方案糟糕，且每况愈下。他们迫切需要行动。这时你要从项目模式转向解决方案模式，作为供应商，要深度参与客户问题。（00:12:54）：从一开始，你就得倾听他们的需求。他们不关心你的产品，只关心自己的问题。这时你要针对性提问，就像看医生时医生不会说："能给您展示我刚做的手术视频吗？"而是会问："请详细描述您的症状。"这才是关键。同样，这种模式比项目型业务更具可扩展性，但扩展上限取决于目标细分市场。（00:13:31）：我们有"保龄球道模式"式的扩展路径。可以拓展到相邻的第二个或第三个细分市场。相邻意味着同一客户不同场景应用，或同一场景应用于不同客户群。前者借助客户参考案例，后者则借助合作伙伴——他们会说："我们还有另一个细分市场，带你一起进来吧。"这样就能让公司从数千万美元级别跃升至数亿美元级别。在计算机辅助设计等专业领域，情况更是如此。
实际上，其价值可能会达到10亿美元甚至更高。（00:14:13）但对于大多数其他品类而言，都会在某个阶段迎来第三个转折点——即当人们意识到“等等，Wi-Fi不只是金融分析师的专属，或者说……Wi-Fi是属于所有人的。”因此，企业不再说“我们认同你的观点”（因为这种策略已经过时了）。而这些用户甚至不再说“我们需要你现有的产品”，他们会说“我们想要他们拥有的服务。这太酷了。我也想要他们提供的服务。”这就形成了我们所说的"龙卷风效应"。龙卷风效应意味着企业需要扩大销售覆盖面、拓宽市场、提供标准化产品，基本目标是尽可能抢占市场份额。相关策略详见《龙卷风之道》一书。（00:15:02）最后一个模式在本世纪变得愈发重要，叫做"主街模式"。在这个模式下，产品已然同质化，服务成为创新的新领域。出租车行业已有百年历史，但Uber却价值非凡。企业需将产品转变为服务，而如何实现服务革命呢？当下人们会说：“我不想拥有产品本身。”比如年轻人会说：“我不想买车，只要能叫Uber就行，多方便啊。”以上四种模式中，《跨越鸿沟》一书重点探讨了第二个模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. You touched on so many things that I want to talk about. I definitely want to dive into the bowling alley metaphor and strategy there. But to close the loop on this target audience to start with initially. First of all, you have this awesome bonfire analogy that I think might be useful to share. Then along that, is there any example or an example or two you could share of just someone that did that really well of picking a really good initial target?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你提到了很多我想探讨的内容。我特别想深入探讨保龄球馆的比喻和相关策略。但首先还是要回归到目标受众这个话题。首先，你提到的篝火比喻很棒，我觉得可以分享给其他人。然后，在这个基础上，能否举个例子，说明如何有效地选定初始目标受众？

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: Sure. Well, the bonfire analogy is just the tendency when you're in the chasm is, "I just need more customers. I should take any customer I could find." Because we need revenue, but the analogy I have is it's like taking a match, and running it back and forth under a log. It's not going to light the log. So how do you start a fire? Well, you start it by putting a little kindling, a little crumpled up paper, and you hold the match one place until the fire starts. Then you want to build... The bowling alley metaphor is a little bit about, first of all, how could you win your first segment, but then increasingly, how would you go forward to win it? That's why adjacency is so important. If you like the fire and the piece of kindling is here, but the log is in the other room, that doesn't work. So I think those are the key ideas. (00:16:59): There's a lot of people that have made Crossing the Chasm successful. The one that we wrote about first was this company called Documentum, and it's a good example. So it was a document management database back in the day that was not... that nobody had any, "Why would you need this?" It started with the pharmaceutical industry, because pharma said, "Well, new drug approvals are 500,000 page documents, and they really, really, really are hard to manage, and we're screwing it up. And every day we screw it up, we lose a day of patent life of our drug, and the day of patent life's worth about a million or $2 million a day. This is a bad situation. We need to do something." (00:17:37): So "Okay, pharma, you got pharma." Great. Well, then what happened was the guys in petrochemicals said, "Well, we're in the chemical industry. We're not in the pharmaceutical industry, but we have these standard operating manuals, and we have all these regulatory demands on us too. Not quite like the FDA, but this looks like this could be pretty useful to us too." And then after the petrochemicals guys got... Well, the chemical guys got it, then the petrochemical guys got it. Of course, they're oil and gas, and they say, "Well, in addition, we have all these leases. The lease holds them. It's brilliant. This property is critical to our future plan, so we need a document database for the leases." (00:18:20): So the guys on Wall Street who are financing these guys are going, "Well, wait a minute. Hell, I mean, we're paper from wall to wall here. Why don't we..." So what happens is you have this thing of this expansion, but in each case, it was into a new segment, but the use cases were close enough.
turns.zh: 当然。篝火比喻主要讲的是，当你身处鸿沟阶段时，人们往往会想：“我只需要更多客户，应该不择手段地获取客户。” 因为我们需要营收，但我的比喻是，就像拿着一根火柴，在木头下来回摩擦。根本点不着火。所以如何点火呢？首先要放一点引火物，比如揉皱的纸片，然后把火柴固定在一个位置，直到火势渐起。保龄球馆比喻主要讲的是，首先如何赢得第一个细分市场，然后如何逐步扩展。邻近效应非常重要。如果火源和引火物在另一个房间，就无法成功。所以这些都是关键理念。（00:16:59）：有很多公司成功应用了《跨越鸿沟》理论。我们最先写到的是Documentum公司，这是个很好的例子。当时它是一家文档管理数据库公司，但没人看好，人们觉得“为什么需要这个？”它最初针对制药行业，因为制药公司说：“新药审批文件有50万页，管理起来极其困难，浪费了大量时间。每天效率低下，药物专利保护期就缩短一天，而每一天的专利保护期价值约100万至200万美元。这太糟糕了，必须采取措施。” （00:17:37）：然后石化行业的人说：“我们虽然不在制药行业，但也有标准操作手册和监管要求，虽然不像FDA那么严格，但也能派上用场。” 接着石化行业的人掌握后，化学品行业的人又跟进。当然，石油和天然气行业的人说：“我们还有租约管理，这些租约对未来规划至关重要，所以需要租约数据库。” （00:18:20）：华尔街的投资者也参与进来：“等等，别急，我们这里文件堆积如山，何不……” 所以这种扩张模式在每个阶段都是针对新细分市场，但用例必须足够相似。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So if a startup founder is listening and trying to decide is their initial target audience, their ICP too wide, do you have any advice for how to know if this is still too wide, and you should try to get more and more narrow? I know you talk about a single use case. What else should people be thinking about there?
turns.zh: 如果有创业者想知道自己的初始目标受众或ICP是否太宽泛，你有什么建议？你提到要聚焦单一用例，还有其他需要考虑的方面吗？

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: Well, so first of all, before you try to cross the chasm, do you have a marquee? Have you won a marquee customer that puts you on the map? Because if you're not... You need to make yourself visible before you can make the Crossing the Chasm play. Let's assume you've done that. So then when we first saw, "Well, why don't I just use that industry?" Turns out that the visionary person you work with... First of all, they did some very weird things because they're visionaries and second of all, they don't want to help their industry. The whole point of this was they wanted to get ahead of their competitors. They didn't want to help. So normally you can't use the visionary project as your beachhead. You'd love to from a point of view of reusing the work. You just can't. So then the question becomes, "Okay, where am I going to go?" (00:19:41): So the key formula, and this is the formula... If there's one sort of takeaway from founders listening at this point, you want to have a target segment that is big enough to matter, small enough to lead and a good fit with your crown jewels. That's the formula. So big enough to matter means do I have enough room to double or... Often venture capitalists talk about a triple double followed by a double triple. So if you said, "Okay, let's just, I'm going to make you a million dollars." Put that visionary, but just to give you a number. Okay, so a double triple would be I went from one to four and from four to 12, and then I did a triple double. So that would be 12 to 24, 24 to 48, 48 to 90. Okay, so how would you get from one to a hundred million dollars? (00:20:31): So you want to have a segment that says that I could get to a hundred million dollars in a five year... That was a five-year window. So you say, "Okay, but what it can't be is a billion dollar segment." Because if it's a billion dollar segment, you might be able to get there, but you would not be a big fish. So that's a fish to pond ratio thing. So you want to think about, particularly as you're starting out... This is a B2B model predominantly. If I could take the top 20 customers in this segment, meaning... What do I mean by a segment? It's in the same geography. People in Japan don't talk to people in America. People in America don't talk to people in Germany, they even speak different languages. I don't know why everybody doesn't speak English, but apparently they don't. So they have to be same geography, same industry, because dentists do not talk to software designers, who don't talk to advertising people and in the same profession. (00:21:23): So salespeople don't talk to finance people and finance people don't talk to the guys in the warehouse. So same industry, same geography, same profession. And then the compelling use case, which is the thing... That's the thing that starts the fire. There's segments everywhere and by the way, they all have that... They all do... Every segment works the same way. If I have to make a high risk buying decision, I'm going to talk to my peers about it. And I don't want to be first. I want to be able to do whatever the herd's doing. But what a compelling reason to buy does is it goes well, but I have to act faster than I want to. And that's what you need as an entrepreneur. You need the customer to be coming toward you even though you're new and you're unproven, and frankly you scare the crap out of them, but they're even more afraid of the problem that they're saddled with. So that's why you can build a relationship with them.
turns.zh: 嗯，首先，在你尝试跨越鸿沟之前，你有客户案例吗？你是否赢得了一个能让你的品牌声名远扬的客户？因为如果没有的话……你需要先让自己被看到，才能实施“跨越鸿沟”的策略。假设你已经做到了这一点。那么当我们最初看到“好吧，为什么不直接利用这个行业呢？”的时候。结果发现，与你合作的那个有远见的人……首先，他们做了一些非常奇怪的事情，因为他们是梦想家；其次，他们不想帮助自己的行业。整个策略的核心在于，他们想领先竞争对手，不想去帮助别人。所以通常你不能把这个有远见的项目当作你的滩头阵地。尽管你从重用现有工作的角度出发很想这么做，但你就是做不到。于是问题就来了：“好吧，那我该往哪儿走？”（00:19:41）：所以关键公式是……如果听众中有创业者能从中领悟到一点，那就是：你需要一个目标细分市场，这个市场要足够大到有意义，足够小到能引领，并且与你的核心产品高度契合。这就是公式。所谓“足够大到有意义”，意思是我们是否有足够的空间实现翻倍增长……通常风险投资家会谈到“三倍翻倍，再加两倍翻倍”。假设你说：“好吧，让我给你一个例子。”你可以拿出一个有远见的项目，但只是举个数字。好吧，那么三倍翻倍就是从1增长到4，再从4增长到12，然后再三倍翻倍。所以从1增长到1亿美元要怎么做？（00:20:31）：所以你需要一个细分市场，要能让你在五年内达到1亿……这是一个五年的窗口期。所以你说：“好吧，但它不能是一个10亿美元的细分市场。”因为如果是一个10亿美元的细分市场，你或许能做到，但你就不是大鱼了。所以这是一个鱼与池塘的比例问题。尤其是在你刚起步的时候……这主要是B2B模式。如果我能拿下这个细分市场的前20个客户，意味着……我说的“细分市场”是什么意思？它要在同一地理区域内。日本人不和美国人交流，美国人不和德国人交流，他们甚至说不同的语言。我不知道为什么大家不都说英语，但显然他们不说。所以他们必须在同一地理区域、同一行业、同一专业内。然后是引人注目的用例，这才是……点燃火花的东西。到处都有细分市场，顺便说一下，它们都有……每个细分市场都遵循同样的模式。如果我要做一个高风险购买决策，我会和同行讨论这个问题。我不想成为第一个。我想做大家都在做的事。但一个引人注目的购买理由会带来好处，但我必须比自己想的更快行动。这就是你作为创业者需要的。你需要客户主动向你靠近，尽管你是新手、未经证实的，坦白说他们会被你吓到，但他们更害怕被困在现有问题中。所以这就是为什么你能和他们建立关系的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And this phase comes... You kind of imply it comes after, say you're at a million dollars AR, you don't do this sort of work of trying to cross the chasm at that point, until you reach something like that?
turns.zh: 太棒了。然后这个阶段就来了。。。你有点暗示它是在之后才出现的，比如说当你的AR收入达到一百万美元时，你不会在那个时候就开始尝试跨越鸿沟，而是要等到达到某个更高的水平？

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: I'm not sure AR is going to be the right reference. Here's what you need. You need a major account who's gone all in with you on the new technology and who is willing in some way to talk about it. The good news about visionaries is they tend to have fairly big egos and they tend to like to talk, unlike pragmatists who will not want to talk. Pragmatists, they'll have to go to legal and get permission and blah, blah, blah. But once you've got that, whatever your revenue is at that point, you should be starting to think about, "Well, what is my beachhead segment?" And the good news about Crossing the Chasm, it's not expensive. (00:23:12): Think about it, once you've said, I'm going to stay in one geography, in one industry, one profession, think about your marketing budget. You're not buying Super Bowl ads here. There's no sock puppets. That's not what we're doing. We want to get to maybe 200 people with a message. And then do you have the domain expertise to really understand the problem? And if it's a really compelling problem, they'll take the meeting and getting that meeting is... Because if you're an entrepreneurial founder, you're probably fairly charismatic. First of all, you've convinced your spouse that you're willing to work for no money with no benefits, and maybe you pitched a venture capitalist and you fooled them, so why can't you fool these guys? Anyway, that would be the way I would go.
turns.zh: 我不确定AR是否是合适的参照。关键在于你需要一个主要客户，他们全力支持新技术，并愿意公开谈论它。关于愿景派的好处是，他们通常比较自信，喜欢与人交流，不像实用派那样不愿开口。实用派需要经过法律部门批准之类的。但一旦你有了这样的客户，无论你当时的收入是多少，都应该开始思考：“好吧，我的突破性市场是什么？”而跨越鸿沟的策略成本不高（00:23:12）：想想看，一旦你决定只专注于一个地理区域、一个行业或一个职业领域，考虑一下你的营销预算。你又不是要买超级碗广告位。没有虚假账号。我们要做的是让大约200人了解我们的信息。然后你是否有足够的专业知识来真正理解问题？如果这是一个非常引人注目的问题，客户会愿意与你会面。而要获得这样的会面并不难。毕竟，如果你是一位创业者，可能相当有魅力。首先，你说服了配偶接受零薪无福利的工作，还成功说服了风险投资家，所以为什么不能说服这些客户呢？总之，这就是我的思路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Essentially, the advice here is if you're a new early stage startup, one of the biggest milestones you want to aim for is a big marquee customer. When I think about this and look at a startup deck, if I see something like Figma is using this product or notion or Salesforce. Clearly, I'll be like, "Wow, okay, these really sophisticated people decided this was useful to them." And so I will innately trust that. There's also often advice of don't work with big companies because they'll push you around, they'll take a long time, they'll force you to build a thing just for them and it won't apply to other people. What's your advice to avoid that downside?
turns.zh: 本质上，建议是，如果你是一家新兴初创公司，最重要的里程碑之一就是获得一个大客户。当我审视初创公司的商业计划书时，如果看到Figma、Notion或Salesforce在使用你的产品，我会惊叹：“哇，真的吗？这些成熟的公司都认为这个产品对他们有用。”我会自然而然地信任它。然而，人们常建议不要与大公司合作，因为它们会把你当成棋子，耗费大量时间，迫使你为它们定制产品，而这些产品对其他人毫无用处。如何避免这种弊端？

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: It has to do with the persona of the executive sponsor. Nine out of 10 executive sponsors are going to be the negative because they're going to be a company person working with company processes. They're going to send you to purchasing, nobody's going to be happy. You're looking for the 10th one. The 10th one is one who says, "I'm so tired of the status quo. I'm looking for people that are visionary like me. I like talking to you better than I like talking to my peers because you're different and I want to be different. I want to leapfrog the world, and these people just want to stay on the escalator. So they're staying on the escalator. God bless them, but I want to jump over the top." So it's a persona based choice is the key thing there.
turns.zh: 关键在于执行赞助人的个性。十个执行赞助人中有九个会是消极的，因为他们是公司职员，受制于公司流程。他们会把你推给采购部门，没有人会满意。你要找到第十个。第十个会说：“我厌倦了现状。我在寻找像我一样有远见的人。我更愿意和你交流，而不是和同行交谈，因为你与众不同，我也想与众不同。我想引领世界，而他们只想随波浮沉。所以他们就随波浮沉吧，上帝保佑他们，但我想跳出框架。” 所以，选择一个有远见的执行赞助人是关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting. And then say that you are an early stage startup again, how soon do you think it makes sense to invest in finding that big marquee customer versus finding some smaller... I imagine you start with some startups to see how people... You don't go straight there.
turns.zh: 这真的很有趣。再说回初创公司，你觉得在多早的时候投资寻找大客户比寻找小客户更有意义？我猜你会先与一些初创公司合作，看看人们的反应...你不会直接就去找大客户。

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: Yes, and so initially, I think... And of course you and I are both playing, let's be clear, we're playing a software game. For example, I was trying to apply this framework to Intel, and Intel said to me, "Geoffrey, you do understand that a prototype product in our industry costs about $500 million." Okay, okay, okay, okay. Maybe that's not the same model. I think in our world right now with digital transformation, most entrepreneurs are doing some software led play, which means you can work with a small team. So I think what I would advise is I would do projects. Even though I have a product vision, I would start with trying to make as much projects, which would be very customer led. And frankly, initially, even if I have a roadmap, the customer's probably going to take me off my roadmap a bit. (00:26:31): I'd have to be willing to say, "I'm going to open the aperture enough." Because I just need to get enough experience with the technology. I need to put in people's hands. If it's a freemium play, you can do it for free. But that tends to be more of a consumer play. There are exceptions. There are B2B companies like Atlassian and things that did start as a freemium play, but that's not as normal. I would think more of the consultative play to do that. But what I would try to do, so I would try to get to cashflow break even on my own money with no venture capital. The only reason you need venture capital is if... Well, two things. Either A, the technology is too expensive and you cannot self-fund it, GPUs a bunch of that, training large language modules, those kinds of things. Or this thing is going to catch fire too soon and I don't have time to dither around for two or three years. So those are two reasons to go to venture capital, but just because you want to do a startup doesn't mean you need venture capital.
turns.zh: 是的，首先，我认为……当然，你我都在参与这场游戏，说白了，我们玩的是软件游戏。比如，我曾试图将这个框架应用于英特尔，而英特尔对我说：“杰弗里，你要明白，在我们这个行业，原型产品动辄就需要5亿美元的成本。”好吧好吧好吧好吧。或许这不是同一个模式。我认为在当前的数字化转型浪潮中，大多数创业者都在进行软件主导的创新，这意味着你可以用小团队就能开展业务。所以我的建议是，先做项目。即便我有产品愿景，也要先尝试开发尽可能多的客户导向型项目。坦白说，最初即便我有路线图，客户也可能会把我带离既定轨道。我必须愿意说：“我要把格局放得足够大。”因为我只需要积累足够的技术经验，把产品交到用户手中。如果是免费增值模式，你可以免费提供服务，但这通常更适用于消费级应用。也有例外，比如Atlassian这样的B2B公司，它们最初就是以免费增值模式起步的，但这种情况并不常见。我更倾向于采取咨询式策略来实现这一目标。但我会努力做到，用自己的资金就能实现现金流收支平衡，无需风险投资。需要风险投资的唯一原因是……嗯，两个方面。要么A，技术成本过高，无法自筹资金，比如GPU、训练大型语言模块之类的技术投入；要么B，项目会迅速爆发，但你没有两三年时间去慢慢探索。所以这两个原因才是求助风险投资的理由，但仅仅因为想创业并不意味着就必须依赖风险投资。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We had Jason Fried on recently the CO of Basecamp, and he made that point in many different ways. The benefits of not raising and how most VC funded companies do not work out, and even though they do, you often don't make as much as you could if you tried it to bootstrap it. So I think there's a lot of resonance there. And you have this quote that essentially kind of what you just said, that with a single round of funding, you should be able to cross the chasm and dominate a single use case in a single market within 18 to 24 months.
turns.zh: 我们最近邀请了Basecamp的首席运营官杰森·弗里德（Jason Fried），他从多个角度阐述了这一观点。比如不融资的好处，以及多数风投支持的公司最终难逃失败的命运。即便成功了，如果能自力更生，也能创造更大的价值。比如GPU、大规模语言模型训练等技术投入，成本实在过高。这类项目往往发展过快，而你又没有两三年时间慢慢摸索。所以这两个原因才是求助风投的理由，但仅仅因为想创业并不意味着就必须依赖风投。

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: Yeah. This is like an English major doing math, so be careful because I am an English major. But in general, because again, I said it's not expensive, and by the way, you're not discounting. In other words, you're actually using value pricing because the problem you're solving is severe enough, the customer doesn't want a discount, the customer wants you to... It is like if you have to have heart surgery, you don't want a coupon that says, "Heart surgery 9.99 this Saturday only." You want to go to the Mayo Clinic or you want to go to wherever, so you don't have to discount. (00:28:44): What you do have to do is you have to make almost like a guaranteed commitment to the problem to solve. We're going to take this problem off the table and we're not leaving until you're satisfied. That's the key to the game. That's a little bit weird because if you've invented ChatGPT, and now you're saying, "But I am going to solve the third grade math problem," which is a real problem. But ChatGPT can do anything. I know, but we're going to solve the third grade math problem. That's hard for a lot of entrepreneurs to get their head around.
turns.zh: 是啊。这就像英语专业的学生做数学题一样，所以要小心点，因为我就是英语专业出身的。但总的来说，因为我之前说过价格不贵，顺便说一句，你们又没有打折。换句话说，你们实际上是在用价值定价，因为你们解决的问题足够严重，客户不需要折扣，他们需要你去……就像如果你需要做心脏手术，你肯定不想看到一张优惠券写着“本周六仅需9.99美元的心脏手术优惠”。你会想去梅奥诊所或者其他地方，所以没必要打折。（00:28:44）：你们必须要做的是，对解决的问题做出几乎是百分之百的承诺。我们要把这个问题彻底解决，直到客户满意为止。这才是关键所在。这有点奇怪，因为如果你发明了ChatGPT，现在却说要去解决三年级数学题——这可是个实实在在的问题。但ChatGPT无所不能。我知道，但我们就要解决三年级数学题。这对很多创业者来说都难以理解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of the way Figma started, even though it took them a long time to find product market fit and started scaling, they ended up working very closely with Coda. I don't know if you know the story where they just wanted to make sure the Coda team, and it was called Krypton back then was very happy with Figma. So they went to the office, they set them all up, they started using Figma. And then on the drive home they called him like, "It doesn't work anymore. Something's broken." And they were already home. And Dylan basically, and this team drove all the way back, I think it was an hour or two, and got there and turned out the Wi-Fi was down and there was some internet issue and fixed it and just was obsessed with making sure they were using it. And they're also just fixing the most ridiculous bugs that were not important because they just wanted to make sure they were really happy with it.
turns.zh: 这让我想起了Figma的起步历程。尽管他们花了很长时间才找到产品市场匹配点并开始规模化扩张，但最终他们与Coda合作得非常紧密。我不知道你是否了解这个故事，他们当时只想确保Coda团队（当时叫Krypton）对Figma满意。所以他们去了办公室，把所有设备都安装好，开始使用Figma。然后在回家的路上，他们打电话给他说：“现在用不了了。出了点问题。”而他们当时已经到家了。迪伦基本上带领团队驱车一两个小时赶回去，结果发现是Wi-Fi断了，网络出了问题，然后就立刻去解决，执着于确保用户能正常使用。同时，他们还会修复那些看似微不足道的bug，只因为他们想确保用户真正满意。

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: [inaudible 00:30:11] a larger company would say, "Look, we'll put you in our queue and you'll be on our... We'll get to you." I think this is... And by the way, this is part of the fun, frankly, of being in a startup because you're so close to the action, because there's nothing between you and the action. So why wouldn't you do that?
turns.zh: [00:30:11不可听清]一家大公司可能会说：“看，我们会把你排进队列，等轮到你。”我觉得这……说实话，这正是创业的乐趣所在，因为你离行动太近了，没有任何阻隔。所以为什么不这样做呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and I think one of the takeaways I've had for my own research into this is that you need to find one company that just loves you. It's not like "[inaudible 00:30:37], this is cool." It's like, "I love this product. I would never want to give it up."
turns.zh: 是啊，我从自己的研究中得出的一个关键点是，你需要找到一家真正喜欢你的公司。不是那种“嗯，这很酷”的态度，而是“我爱死这个产品了。我绝对不想放弃它。”

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: That's kind of what I meant by that marquee ref... We sometimes we call it a radiating reference. It's just somebody really, we talk about you when you're not even in the room. Yeah, very cool.
turns.zh: 这就是我所说的引荐效应……我们有时称之为辐射式推荐。就是有人真心实意地在你不在场的时候谈论你。这太酷了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We've talked about this idea of the chasm and Crossing the Chasm, but it might be helpful just to explain what is the idea, what is this chasm? What is it that people fall into and why is this important?
turns.zh: 我们讨论过“鸿沟”和“跨越鸿沟”的概念，但或许有必要先解释一下什么是“鸿沟”？人们为什么会陷入这个鸿沟？为什么这很重要？

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: And this was funny, because I was working at Regis McKenna, which was this marketing agency that was sort of the premier high-tech marketing agency in the eighties. And we had all these really successful launches, and then covers of front page articles on Fortune magazine and Wall Street Journal. And then a couple of years later it's like, "Well, what happened to these guys?" So that's where the chasm was like... That's what caused the investigation. What we learned was visionaries make their own buying decisions, and they do not consult their peers. In fact, if their peers are doing it, they're probably not going to do it because they want to be different. So basically these companies were having success capturing the imagination of the visionary, and they thought, "Well, I'll use the visionaries as a reference to get the pragmatist." (00:31:53): The pragmatist looks at the visionary and goes, "That's not my guy. First of all, he thinks I'm dumb. He thinks he's smarter than I am. Second of all, he does stuff that I would never do, and he makes decisions in a way that I would never make them. So that's not... No. So but I am interested in talking to my peers, but the problem now is, well, which of the peers are going to go first?" And it was kind of like the junior high dance problem. How do you get the party started? So that was the chasm. That was what created the chasm. The pragmatists need references and they will not accept a visionary as a reference, and they don't have any peers that have tried it yet. So that was what was happening.
turns.zh:
这一点很有趣，因为我当时在雷吉斯·麦肯纳公司工作。这家营销公司在八十年代堪称高科技营销领域的领军者。我们成功策划了多个产品发布，相关报道还登上了《财富》杂志和《华尔街日报》的头版。然而几年后，人们开始疑惑："这些人后来怎么了？" 这正是引发分歧的根源所在——调查发现，有远见卓识的人往往会按照自己的标准做决策，而非参考同行的意见。事实上，如果同行在做某件事，他们往往会反其道而行之，彰显独特个性。

（00:31:53）：务实派会审视有远见的人并评价道："这不是我要找的人。首先，他觉得我很笨。他自以为比我聪明。其次，他做的事我绝不会尝试，决策方式也与我背道而驰。" 这就是分歧所在。分歧的根源在于务实派需要可靠的参考案例，却不认可有远见者的推荐，同时身边又没有成功案例可供借鉴。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's such an important point that I think people don't quite always get that that reference, marques customer needs to be a pragmatist. It can't be one of these early adopters that are just trying stuff. And these other pragmatists need to feel that this is my person, this is just like me. And they love it.
turns.zh: 我认为这一点至关重要，但人们往往忽视了客户需要务实派这一点。客户不应是那些盲目追随潮流的早期采用者，而应是能与自己产生共鸣的同行，他们要能感受到"这就是我要找的人"，并真心认同产品价值。

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: By the way, one of the reasons that pragmatists have a certain... It's not contempt for visionaries, but it's definitely wariness, it's because often they have to clean up the messes that these guys leave behind because when you're a visionary, you leave a lot of messes in your wake. And then the pragmatist has to come in and clean it up. So they're going, "Oh, that's another mark against these people."
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，务实派对有远见者存在警惕心理，并非轻视——因为有远见者常留下烂摊子，务实派往往不得不收拾残局。这让务实派不禁质疑："这些人真不靠谱。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I saw a deck of yours where you actually represent each of these stages of the lifecycle and the visionary Steve Jobs is the way you represented it, and the pragmatists are just like business people in suits sitting at a conference table.
turns.zh: 我曾看到你的演示文稿，里面用不同角色代表产品生命周期的不同阶段。你把史蒂夫·乔布斯描绘成有远见者，而务实派则像是西装革履的商务人士围坐在会议桌旁。

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: Exactly. And there's six of them. And the key idea behind that is none of us... By the way, I don't think any of these people are a guru and they don't think I'm a guru. We're using the antelope strategy, it's a herd strategy. But at some point... And by the way, we do this all the time, every one of... Airbnb, I want to get an Airbnb in Portland. Have you ever stayed [inaudible 00:33:53]? Is this a good hotel? Is this a good restaurant? Is this a good dentist? Is this a good lawyer? That's how we do it.
turns.zh: 没错。共有六个阶段。关键在于，我们都不是孤军奋战——顺便说一句，我认为这些人里没人是大师，他们也不认为我是大师。我们采用的是羚羊战略，即群体策略。但在某个节点……顺便说一句，我们日常也常这么做。比如："我想在波特兰订个Airbnb。你在那住过吗？这家酒店好吗？这家餐厅好吗？这位牙医靠谱吗？这位律师靠谱吗？"这就是我们的决策方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think Uber and Airbnb is the best example of this in action where I would not ride in a random car, especially I think women were most like, "I will never get into a car, into an Uber." This is insane until all of their friends are doing it. And then, "Okay, let's give it a shot."
turns.zh: 我认为Uber和Airbnb就是这一理论在现实中的最佳范例。我绝不会随便搭陌生人的车，尤其是女性往往会说：“我绝对不会坐Uber。”这种想法在朋友们都开始尝试后才慢慢改变，最终她们会说：“好吧，就试试看吧。”

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: I guess it's okay, yeah.
turns.zh: 我觉得也还好啦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So essentially most people were pragmatists and I guess that makes sense. And pragmatists make up the biggest chunk for it.
turns.zh: 是啊。所以说大多数人都是实用主义者，这其实挺合理的。实用主义者构成了这类创新的主力军。

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: And by the way, you can be a visionary with some things, a pragmatist with other things, and a conservative with other things. So the way to really think about them is, what is my persona in relation to this decision?
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，有些事你可以当个梦想家，有些事当个实用主义者，有些事当个保守派。关键在于，面对某个决策，你的角色定位是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this example of the junior high dance problem where nobody wants to go ask the person. It's like, "I'm going to wait for them to come to me. I want to see how this plays out." It's such a good metaphor. In terms of how much of your product needs to be built at each of these stages. What advice do you share? How much do you need for these visionaries versus the next?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢初中舞会那个例子，没人愿意主动去邀请对方。他们会说：“我就等着他们来找我，看看结果如何。”这个比喻太贴切了。在产品发展的不同阶段，需要投入的资源也不同。对这类梦想家和普通用户，应该分别给予怎样的支持？

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: So with a visionary, you have to have the magic ingredient working. You don't have the whole product. And in fact, your product may be buggy, but it does something... Andy Grove used to call it the 10 x effect. You need to do something that is an order of magnitude better than anything because that's why the visionary is talking to you. They're going, "Oh my gosh, you have this fusion." "Fusion, really?" "Yeah, we got fusion energy." So that's number one. Then what would still cause you to not cross the chasm yet? If there's not enough product there, pragmatists cannot put up with a product that doesn't work. So you may need to do some additional work to say, "Look, we get some more customers. I'm still living hand to mouth. It's mostly project work, but until the product has got enough stability and can be productized, I really can't afford to cross the chasm." So once you have a product that works, then you've got to say, "Okay, now I've got to find a market where it can be the dominant solution." That's the time to cross the chasm.
turns.zh: 对梦想家来说，关键在于产品得有核心吸引力。产品可能还不够完善，但至少得有核心竞争力。安迪·格鲁夫把这称为10倍效应。你必须提供比现有方案好十倍的解决方案，这样梦想家才会跟你谈：“天哪，你掌握了核聚变技术！”“核聚变？真的吗？！”“是啊，我们成功研发出核聚变能源了。”这就是第一阶段。那么接下来为何还没跨越鸿沟？如果产品功能不完善，实用主义者根本无法忍受不稳定的体验。所以你可能需要完善产品，说：“看，我们又吸引了新用户，但目前还是在赚小钱，主要靠项目维持，但产品稳定后才能实现商业化。”这时候才能跨越鸿沟。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And a big part of that is obviously they have bosses, they have checklists, they have compliance people, they have IT people, they have people that need to buy into this or this meeting room with six people. They all have to be like, "All right, this is the best choice."
turns.zh: 关键在于，他们有老板、流程清单、合规人员、IT团队，所有人都得达成共识，甚至召开六人会议讨论。大家必须齐心协力说：“好吧，这是最佳选择。”

turns.speaker: Geoffrey Moore
turns.en: And by the way, normally those people are designed to keep you out, and that decision process will take forever and you'll be in the welfare lines before they make their choice. So that's why it's so important to have what we call the compelling reason to buy. You need to have a group of people in a room where the leader, the guy who's going to actually sponsor make this decision is saying, "Look, I already gave this problem to everybody in the room, and our answer sucks." He wouldn't say it that way, but that's the truth. And therefore, we're kind of at the... I mean, I'm getting the message. First of all, my boss's boss's boss knows my name. That's a very bad thing. Secondly, I'm getting the message, you're either going to fix this problem, Geoffrey, or we're going to find somebody who can. So that's what gives them the energy to go against the inertial momentum of the decision-making process in their company.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，通常那些人就是为了把你拒之门外，而且这个决策过程会拖拖拉拉，你还没来得及排到福利队列，他们就已经做出决定了。所以拥有我们所说的"迫切购买理由"至关重要。你需要让一群人在会议室里，由那个真正要赞助的领导者说道："看，我已经把这个问题交给在座的每一个人了，但我们的解决方案太糟糕了。"他当然不会这么说，但这就是事实。因此，我们正处于……我是说，我已经领会到了。首先，我老板的老板的老板知道我的名字。这很糟糕。其次，我领会到了，如果你不解决这个问题，杰弗里，我们就会找能解决的人。所以这给了他们力量，去对抗公司决策过程的惯性势头。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me tell you about a product called arcade.
